It continues the series’ emphasis on licensed teams, realistic presentation, and competitive online play, particularly in modes like Ultimate Team, Career Mode, and Clubs.

It is primarily experienced as a live-service adjacent sports platform. Most engagement is driven by seasonal content resets, roster updates, and ongoing online competition rather than a fixed narrative or standalone progression. The game’s lifecycle is defined by annual iteration, meaning players typically migrate forward each release cycle rather than staying within a single version long-term.

Its strengths are authentic presentation, strong licensing coverage, and responsive core gameplay that supports both casual and competitive play. However, it is often criticized for incremental yearly changes, heavy monetization in Ultimate Team, and a gameplay loop that can feel familiar across iterations.

Overall, EA SPORTS FC 26 functions as a competitive football simulation platform rather than a traditional game with long-term narrative depth. It is best suited for players invested in online competition, squad building, and yearly sports progression.

100+ hours of gameplay.
To begin with, I must emphasize that my review comes strictly from the perspective of a Manager Career and Player Career player. I have never accessed, nor do I ever intend to access, the Ultimate Team mode. I purchased the latest edition, FC 26, largely based on the promises made regarding improvements to Career Mode. From day one, I noticed a glaring bug: the game calls an offside on passes between two players who have already past the opponent's last defender (I deliberately didn't report this bug just to see how long it would take them to fix it—and it still hasn't been patched to this day). The AI implemented in this version is extremely limited and completely lacks consistency and realism. They didn't bother at all to give the AI basic logic based on real-world player or manager data, leading to transfers that make absolutely no sense. Inexperienced, low-quality players demand to be starters, and in-game events are extremely rare and meaningless. The transfer system is highly impractical, and basic features are missing—like the fact that opposing team players should already be scouted prior to a direct match. Youth academies are completely OP and unrealistic; getting players with 90+ potential is trivial and way too easy. The transition from the youth squad to the first team is too effortless, and their contract demands are utterly unrealistic.

Despite all of this, the biggest disappointment remains the Simulation (Authentic) mode. While the highest difficulty in Competitive mode poses no challenge at all and is extremely easy to beat (a real issue in itself), the situation is the exact opposite in Simulation mode. On Professional difficulty, you win 6-0 in 90% of cases, but the moment you switch to World Class, your chances of winning drop to under 5%. Possession becomes absolute hell; opposing defenders endlessly pass the ball around without giving you any chance to intercept, leaving you to finish the match with barely 25% possession most of the time. The scripting is extremely obvious! I don't understand the point of scripting in a single-player career mode at all.

5/10.

why EA Sports FC 26 Is One of the Most Frustrating Football Games Ever Made

EA Sports FC 26 was supposed to be the game that finally redeemed the franchise after years of criticism. EA promised better gameplay, improved realism, smarter AI, and a more rewarding experience for players. Instead, many fans feel like they got the exact opposite: a broken, scripted, microtransaction-heavy mess that manages to be both exhausting and repetitive at the same time.

One of the biggest problems with FC 26 is the gameplay itself. Passing feels inconsistent, defenders randomly stop tracking runs, and player switching can feel completely broken during crucial moments. Many players online have complained that simple passes go in the wrong direction while defenders react slower than attackers no matter how highly rated they are. The result is a game where matches often feel determined more by glitches, animations, and luck than actual skill.

The so-called “meta” makes things even worse. Instead of rewarding smart football, FC 26 often rewards unrealistic gameplay tactics like constant spinning, kickoff glitches, and abuse of overpowered mechanics. Players who actually want to build attacks realistically are punished, while people abusing broken mechanics dominate online modes. For a game marketed as a football simulation, it frequently feels more like an arcade exploit competition.

Ultimate Team is another major reason people hate the game. EA continues to push aggressive monetization through endless promos, expensive packs, and constant Squad Building Challenges. Many players feel the game is designed less around football and more around encouraging people to spend money. Some frustrated fans have even described the mode as “a casino game” rather than a sports game. The grind becomes exhausting because no matter how much time players invest, EA constantly releases stronger cards that make previous progress feel pointless.

Technical issues only add fuel to the fire. PC players have reported severe input delay, anti-cheat problems, crashes, and lag that make online matches nearly unplayable. Even after patches, many users say the game still feels sluggish and inconsistent. Nothing destroys a competitive game faster than feeling like your controls are fighting against you.

What frustrates longtime fans most is that this cycle keeps repeating every year. EA markets each new release as revolutionary, but many players believe FC 26 is just another recycled version of previous games with slightly updated graphics and new monetization tactics. Community backlash across forums, Reddit, and social media has been intense, with some fans calling it the worst football game EA has ever made. Even players who initially enjoyed the game eventually admitted that the frustration builds over time as gameplay flaws become impossible to ignore.

To be fair, FC 26 is not completely terrible. Some reviewers praised its visuals, presentation, and improvements to offline modes. But flashy graphics and licensed stadiums cannot save a football game when the gameplay itself feels broken. At its core, players want a game that is fair, responsive, and rewarding. Too often, FC 26 feels scripted, unbalanced, and designed more around engagement metrics than genuine fun.

"Trying to get objective rewards feels like a chore and a punishment rather than a fun challenge. There is no transparent rank check, no fair matchmaking, and no protection for casual players, mostly in Live Events. The matchmaking in Live Events (like World Tour Silver Superstars) is an absolute nightmare. The system feels completely random and has zero skill-based balancing. As an average player, I am constantly forced to play against much higher skilled players. You can easily go on a 20-game losing streak just trying to complete a simple objective. EA forces you to play these modes if you want to earn objective rewards, but they turn it into a miserable experience by pairing casual players with hardcore, high-tier opponents. EA needs to fix this, because right now, it's completely trash."

Another installment of an awful game.

First, the positives: this year, the game doesn’t feel like it has any completely broken mechanics. Most mechanics seem relatively balanced, and it’s rare to see players consistently exploiting one specific mechanic nowadays.

Negatives
Game Modes

The game feels like it only has two legitimate game modes: Clubs and Ultimate Team. If you plan on playing Career Mode, you’ll quickly become disgusted by how unrealistic and repetitive it gets.

Problems with Clubs

This year, they implemented a slower progression system, preventing players from reaching max level within the first week. That is objectively a good change.

Other additions are also positive, such as allowing players to join up to three different clubs and the ability to enter matches as a substitute. Although the substitute feature is glitchy and can sometimes freeze or crash your game, the idea itself is very good.

However, they removed the ability to message someone directly in your lobby. Sometimes you play with a random teammate who doesn’t have a microphone, and now you basically have to add them as a friend just to send actual messages instead of the default preset nonsense.

Another issue is the AI players in Clubs. It would make sense for them to gradually improve throughout the year. They don’t need to become elite-level players, but at the time of writing this review, the AI is genuinely terrible. Even top players would struggle to defend simple plays because of how bad the AI defenders are.

Regarding Ultimate Team

Ultimate Team is fun at first, but it quickly becomes overly repetitive. The fact that a new promotion drops every single week completely ruins the sense of progression.

Saving coins for a great player doesn’t feel rewarding anymore. You grind endlessly, finally get the player you wanted, and two weeks later their price has dropped by 90%. That’s not healthy for the mode, and it only encourages people to spend real money just to keep up with the constant cycle of content — especially if you actually have a life outside the game, unlike me.

For competitive players, it would also be nice to have proper rankings showing the percentage of players in each Rivals division and FUT Champions rank.

Gameplay

Going back to the positives, I mentioned earlier that no mechanic feels overwhelmingly broken this year. Unfortunately, that’s about the only genuinely positive thing I can say about the gameplay.

The gameplay is wildly inconsistent. Passing — even with players who have excellent passing stats — feels like flipping a coin. You either get a perfect pass or some ridiculous animation that sends the ball straight to the defender.

Dribbling feels unresponsive, and defenders controlled by AI are often better than actual players. Your opponent can simply let the AI defend for them, and it will still do an excellent job. That’s terrible game design.

Crosses and long shots are also almost useless. Crosses are usually floated straight into the goalkeeper’s hands, and outside-the-box shots end up flying into the corner flag 90% of the time if you’re lucky.

Goalkeepers are undeniably better than last year, but they still concede absurd near-post goals far too often.

The tactics system also needs a complete rework. It forces you into specific formations, and the role changes often have very limited impact on gameplay.

Defensive line settings feel completely unrealistic. A “high line” barely pushes beyond midfield, and the moment the opponent attacks, defenders immediately sprint backwards instead of maintaining shape. A low line is even worse — the defenders practically sit inside the goal. Watch an actual football match, developers.

Features that used to exist, like manually adjusting player movement in attack and defense, are gone. On top of that, experimenting with different tactics is basically punished if you want to stay competitive. The “meta” dominates everything, as if we’re playing Call of Duty instead of a football game.

Final Thoughts

To conclude: this is another horrible game from a horrible franchise that has only survived because it has no real competition. Year after year, they continue to deliver mediocre products, and people keep buying them anyway.

Two things to make this game fun for single players. FIFA Mod Manager, and FC26 Live Editor. The mods aren't much in general but it adds a nice touch to things that could be missing for you since EA adds the bare minimum already. FIFA Mod Manager is the dedicated mod manager for FC26. I'd recommend Karika Overhaul which does almost everything if you're missing something you'd like while still just logging on to play offline. The rest of mods are generally UI, kits, players, and soundtracks. FC26 Live Editor makes everything better from player career to manager career. 

First player career
-With FC26 Live Editor, you can adjust your/players stats freely but it'll stay stuck even if you try to change it vanilla. I repeat, the moment you adjust stats through FC26 Live Editor, the vanilla is stuck but changeable through FC26 Live Editor. You can add or remove playstyles, change names of anything of significance to you, change jersey colors, and change anything about a player. Literally. The only downsides are when the game updates to a new version, you'd have to wait a week for it to be free unless you pay $1 to $5 dollars which'll unlock the early access of new updated FC26 Live Editor version 2 to 7 days earlier. If waiting for free then turn steam offline, and update when you get it for free. The amazing person named Aranktu which is his patreon.
-Manager FC26 Live Editor is basically the same thing but I never tested it.

Now actually about the game. I don't see a reason to hate the game besides having to turn on low graphics on pc to make the game actually playable. To make the low settings look better is to lower brightness to 0 and lower contrast to 2-3 with all shadows on. Gameplay depends if you play on authentic(hardcore realism), competitive(arcade), or custom sliders which is what I recommend to get the taste of both worlds. 

Player Career is grindy so that's why I mentioned live editor. Obviously not worth full price or in general, all sports game aren't. It's worth about $20 to $30 at most even with all the licenses. I don't play multiplayer but it looks fun if you're good at the game, and have a good chill team. I'd recommend this game if you like to just chill and play with some trophies at stake. Also this game for the newer rosters.

If you're looking for something more, I'd recommend looking at some at the older titles. FIFA 22/23 for pure banger shots and arcade with better vanilla player career if I can remember. FIFA17/18/19 for just pure classic, and simplicity. Best player careers/journey mode although missing some licenses if I remember.

FC 26 has serious gameplay issues that completely hurt immersion and realism. The biggest problem is the movement system, players constantly glide across the pitch like they’re ice skating instead of moving with proper weight, balance, and momentum. Direction changes happen unnaturally fast, animations blend poorly, and overall movement lacks the grounded feeling you would expect from a football simulation.

Defending feels inconsistent, player reactions are delayed or scripted, and many situations look predetermined rather than dynamic. Dribbling often looks artificial, physical duels lack authenticity, and the ball physics still don’t feel convincing enough for a modern football game.

Visually the game can look good at times, but once you actually play, the gameplay flow breaks the illusion very quickly. Matches rarely resemble real football because the pacing, movement, and AI behavior feel too arcade-like and animation-driven.

EA keeps improving presentation and monetization systems, but the core gameplay still needs major work if the goal is realism

This game is awful. There are 7 difficulty levels and the first 4 difficulty levels you will be winning every match 8-0 or maybe even by double digits sometimes. So you bump it up to the 5th difficulty level (World Class) and then you are slogging it out against psychic defenders that know every move before you make it and you are scrapping for every millimeter in the midfield only for 80% of matches to end in a draw or worse. It is mind boggling that they have 7 difficulty levels and you still can't find one that feels just right.

A bunch of the systems in the game, like passing and shooting and even aspects of the career modes are literally de-evolutions of the systems that were in the FIFA games from 8+ years ago. This series in going backwards in so many ways.

Also, there is clearly some sort of scripting BS going on in the background because things often happen in matches that are just incredibly phony and are obvious that the game just decided to make something happen rather than it feeling like it happened naturally. One extremely obvious example was when I was in a player career playing for Schalke and we played Borussia Dortmund on the final day of the season and had a nice natural feeling game and a win by a small margin. Then for the next season I transferred my player to Bayern Munich and coincidentally my new team was to play Borussia Dortmund on the first game of the season. So I was essentially playing them back to back but now I would be on a better team so I figured I would have an easier time. Instead, it felt like the difficulty level had been turned up 2x, though we were eventually able to go up 2-0, but then they made a comeback right at the end and equalized 2-2. I was determined to win, so I hit Alt-F4 to rage quit and retry. I tried two more times to beat them, but the same thing happened all three times. I would go up 2-0, then they would turn into gods and my defenders would just step aside for them and allow them to equalize 2-2. All 3 times the exact same score line played out in the exact order and with fairly similar timing. What a load of garbage.

I’ve been playing FIFA since 2008, starting on PS2 and continuing all the way to PC. I play EA FC26 almost every day, especially FUT Champions, and honestly the game has become extremely frustrating.

The biggest problem is the gameplay delay and lag. Many matches feel slow and unresponsive. Players take too long to react, passes go in random directions, and defenders sometimes freeze for no reason. Instead of competing against the opponent, it often feels like competing against the servers.

Another major issue is the pack rewards. Despite spending hours grinding objectives, Rivals, and FUT Champions, the rewards are consistently disappointing. It feels unfair seeing casual players pack top-tier cards while dedicated players get almost nothing valuable after weeks of effort.

The gameplay consistency is also a serious concern. There are too many matches where momentum suddenly changes in strange ways. You can dominate the entire game, create more chances, defend well, and then suddenly your players stop performing normally and everything starts favoring the opponent. This makes FUT Champions feel less skill-based than it should be.

What makes this more disappointing is that I genuinely love the FIFA/EA FC series. I’ve supported and played these games for over 15 years, but FC26 often makes loyal players feel ignored. The community has been asking for better servers, more balanced gameplay, and more rewarding progression for years.

EA FC26 has potential, but right now the experience feels more stressful than enjoyable for many competitive players.

I installed FC26 thinking I was about to play football.

What I actually downloaded was a psychological endurance test disguised as a sports game.

First match in, I’m feeling good. Smooth passing, nice buildup, I’m basically Pep Guardiola with a controller. Then minute 89 hits. My defenders suddenly forget what “legs” are, my goalkeeper performs interpretive dance instead of saving the ball, and the opponent scores with what can only be described as a guided missile disguised as a shot.

1–1.

Okay. Fine. We move.

Second match. I go 2–0 up. Confidence? Through the roof. I start doing skill moves I don’t even understand. Then the game decides: “That’s enough happiness for you.” Suddenly every pass I make is magnetically attracted to the opponent. My players turn like cargo ships. Their striker? Teleports. I concede three goals in five in-game minutes.

Controller? Survives, barely. My soul? Left the building.

Let’s talk about AI. My teammates have the spatial awareness of houseplants. They stand perfectly still while I’m being hunted by three defenders like I owe them money. Meanwhile, the opponent’s AI moves like a synchronized dance crew trained by elite ninjas.

And the referees… I’ve seen softer fouls in a pillow factory go uncalled, while I breathe near someone and it’s apparently a war crime.

But the real boss fight? Online matches.

You load in. You see their team. Full meta squad. Everyone moves like they’ve had three energy drinks and a motivational speech. You try to defend. You fail. You question your life choices. You start wondering if football was a mistake as a concept.

By the end of the session, I’m sitting there in silence, staring at the screen, controller in hand, experiencing a full existential crisis. Not because I lost… but because deep down, I know I’m going to queue again.

Because despite everything…

I kind of love it.

It’s toxic. It’s chaotic. It’s emotionally destructive.

And I’ll be back tomorrow.

EA Sports FC 26 delivers a more refined and technically improved football experience, but it ultimately falls short of being a must-play title.

On the pitch, the game shows clear progress. Gameplay feels smoother, with better player movement, improved passing mechanics, and more responsive controls. The addition of different gameplay styles—focused on realism versus competitive play—adds flexibility and makes matches feel more dynamic depending on how you want to play. Visually, the game remains strong, offering high-quality presentation and realistic player models that enhance immersion.

However, outside of gameplay, the experience is less impressive. Many core modes, such as Career Mode and Clubs, see only minimal improvements, making the overall package feel very similar to previous entries. The interface and menu system can feel slow and outdated, which negatively impacts the user experience.

A major drawback is the continued focus on monetization in Ultimate Team. The mode often feels geared toward spending rather than purely skill-based progression, which can be frustrating for players who do not want to invest additional money.

- There are tons of bugs. For example, when trying to claim Season Objective rewards, the game often freezes and forces you to restart.
- After finishing a match and going to the results screen, the game sometimes crashes—and you end up being given a loss.
- Defending is extremely difficult. Your defenders can lose position at any moment, and this happens on both sides.
- In attack, when you trigger players to make runs, they often hesitate or act confused before moving.
- The game lags constantly. Ping randomly spikes to 200+ for no clear reason.
- Objectives are way too grindy and require an unreasonable amount of playtime.
- Pack odds are terrible.
- You encounter cheaters—for example in Rush mode, teammates don’t move at all, or they just kick the ball away whenever they get it. Very frustrating.

Conclusion: Even with a 70%+ discount, I strongly do NOT recommend it.

After spending several hours with FC 26 on PC, I can honestly say this is one of the most frustrating football game experiences I have had in years.

The biggest issue is that it no longer feels like real football. Too many situations feel more like basketball than football: players shielding endlessly with their back to goal, unrealistic dribbling inside the box, constant rebounds, impossible first-touch passes and attackers winning every loose ball as if the game has already decided the outcome.

A huge percentage of goals conceded come from goalkeeper rebounds that fall perfectly to the CPU every time. Defenders often stop tracking runs, fail to react to second balls or simply stand still while the opponent gets an easy tap-in. On higher difficulties, it often feels less like the AI is smarter and more like your own players become worse.

There are also many moments where the game feels heavily scripted. You can immediately tell when the AI suddenly becomes unstoppable: perfect one-touch passing, impossible headers, defenders refusing to move, midfielders becoming slow and unresponsive. It feels like the game takes control away from the player rather than rewarding good football.

On top of that, the PC version is a mess technically. I had multiple launch issues, anti-cheat problems, crashes, stuttering and had to spend hours trying different fixes just to get the game running consistently. For a company of EA's size, this is unacceptable.

There is still some fun to be had in Career Mode and the presentation is decent, but the core gameplay feels artificial, repetitive and frustrating far too often.

Overall, FC 26 feels more like an expensive annual update built around Ultimate Team mechanics than a proper football simulation.

EA Sports FC 26 is… kind of a mixed experience for me. I even said I wasn’t going to buy it, but seeing some players I really like finally getting real faces (like Fermín and Yıldız) made me change my mind.

The game has a lot of bugs, especially outside of matches. I played a bit of Clubs mode with my cousin, and the main menu was completely broken sometimes. Characters would randomly turn into the other person’s character, or just become a cursed version with no arms, or even completely black models. It’s funny at first, but after a while it just feels unpolished.

In terms of gameplay, it’s pretty much the same as FC 25 with a few adjustments here and there. It’s not bad, it’s still that FIFA/FC gameplay, but don’t expect anything revolutionary.

One thing I’ll give credit for is Career Mode, which is actually more fun than in 25. It feels a bit more engaging and worth playing if you’re into offline modes.

But my biggest issue is the performance/graphics. For some reason, the game dies when I try to play on higher settings, even though my PC can easily handle it (I’m talking like 200 FPS on high). Because of that, I’m forced to play on the lowest settings just to avoid crashes, which is really disappointing.

Overall, the game can still be fun, especially with friends, but the bugs and technical issues hold it back a lot. It feels like it needed more time to be polished.

I’m writing this review fully aware that most people won’t read it. Honestly, this is more of a vent — a way to get my frustration out at Canadians and Romanians who clearly don’t watch any football yet somehow dominate the Football gaming market.
1. Defensive AI: The Rollercoaster of Incompetence
At launch, and again after a promo in October, the defensive AI was nerfed. During that brief window, the game actually rewarded manual defending, and I genuinely enjoyed it.
But then EA — in their infinite wisdom — decided the game was “too hard” for the player base that’s been spoon‑fed by overpowered AI defending since FC25. So they buffed AI defending again. And again.
We’re now back to the same nonsense as last year: players sitting on their CDMs, holding RB/R1, and letting Ultimate‑level AI defend for them.
2. Attacking AI: A Masterclass in Uselessness
The attacking AI is somehow even worse. Players make offside runs I never triggered, then refuse to run when I do ask them to. They randomly stop mid‑run without me pressing RB/R1, letting defenders bully them with ease.
It’s baffling how inconsistent and unresponsive the attacking logic is.
3. PlayStyles and Evos: A False Promise
EA claimed stats would matter more this year — we all knew that was a lie.
I’ve built some strong Evos with great all‑round stats, but without the “meta” PlayStyles (which change every update except Bruiser+ and Bruiser), they’re basically pointless.
Unless you can magically create an Evo with every PlayStyle in the game, investing in them is a waste of time.
4. The Meta Monopoly
Every match feels the same.
Van de Ven and Pina have been meta since day one, and EA has done nothing to encourage variety. Now, near the end of the cycle, Cruyff, Wilson, Van de Ven, and Pina are practically permanent fixtures in every squad.
Creativity is dead.
5. DDA: The “Non‑Existent” System We All Experience
EA will always deny DDA exists, but the gameplay tells a different story.
Tackles bounce straight back to opponents. Deflections fall perfectly for them. Interceptions — even with Intercept+ — somehow funnel the ball to the attacker.
Skill moves let players jam through defenders even when you’ve positioned perfectly.
You can do everything right and still get punished because the game decides it’s “their turn.”
6. Shooting and Goalkeeping: Pure Inconsistency
I’ve had good spells with shooting, but the inconsistency is unreal.
Players with 94+ shooting miss clean chances for no reason, while keepers pull off miracle saves.
Meanwhile, my keeper concedes goals even when I’m actively pressuring the attacker.
There’s no logic, no reliability — just chaos.
7. SBCs: Overpriced and Underwhelming
SBCs this year have been expensive with very little reward.
During TOTY especially, store packs protected the high‑rated players, making SBC grinding nearly pointless.
Even now, during Trophy Titans, the packs mostly spit out baby versions of cards — except Shearer, which I didn’t mind — but the real elite cards (Zidane, Ronaldinho, Gullit, Maldini, Henry, etc.) are practically impossible to pack unless you’re extremely lucky or willing to spend a fortune.
Heroes are slightly better due to the smaller pool, but that just means more duplicates. Vialli haunted my packs, along with baby Campbell and Puyol.
For RTG players or anyone who doesn’t want to drop ridiculous money, it’s demoralising to grind for cards that will be outdated the moment a new promo drops — especially with TOTS around the corner.

This is where I’m at right now. Maybe I’ll update this later, but for now, I just needed to get this out after another weekend league ruined by AI defending.
And if you’re wondering why I still play?
Because, sadly, this is the only football game I can somewhat enjoy. I’m not a fan of Coinami’s gameplay model, and UFL is still too young and too microtransaction‑heavy to be a real alternative.

This review will be exclusive to career mode. It's the only mode I play, I don't have any interest in entertaining EA's famously unacceptable servers for online play, and the very thought of entering the pay to win gambling hell hole of  FUT makes me wish for nuclear winter. Career mode is bad. The choices you make are unsatisfying, frustratingly limited, and are made to feel utterly meaningless by the bafflingly bad gameplay.

The single most glaring flaw with this game is the opponent AI and playstyle. Every single opponent you will play against in career mode will play the exact same type of football, present you with the exact same challenges, and be exploitable in the exact same way. The system you play, the style you choose to adopt, and the style of play you are told to expect from the opponent going into a match have absolutely no impact on how the game will play out. Let me illustrate how every game plays out:
1. kick off. You pass back to your midfield or defence and begin planning your build up play. Or if the opponent kicks off, they boot the ball off the pitch near your goal for a throw in. Remember that thing PSG did a few times in the champions league? Every team from Barnet to Barcelona does it now too.
2. Attempt to play through the opponent. If like me, you get bored out of your mind from dominating every game 8-0 while zoned out on a YouTube video on your second monitor, you'll need to be set to World Class difficulty or above. Anything below that provides no challenge at all. The gap however between Professional and World Class is staggering. Players who can't make a 5 yard pass and run away scared at the sight of the ball on professional, turn into heat seeking missiles and dribbling gods on World Class and above. In this step then, inevitably, slow build up play leads to unrelenting pressing, and quick loss of possession. Oh well, at least we tried to play realistic football!
3. Defending. At this point you might as well top up your water, reply to your emails, and start shaming your brain into going to bed. Once the opponent has the ball, any fun you might have been experiencing goes out the window. First time passes with pin point accuracy. Unstoppable dribbling. Endless recycling of possession. When the opponent tackles you, it's with the accuracy and speed of that one arrow Legolas shoots into the head of a goblin in Moria. When you try to tackle the opponent, it's like Legolas trying to kill that suicide Uruk-hai at the battle of helms deep. You will not win the ball. It doesn't matter who you are playing, they will play pure possession terrorball. For most of this phase of the game, the AI puts you under no pressure, it will rarely attempt to score a goal. It passes around you like your big brother humiliating you, as you flail around trying desperately to win the ball back. Every team in the game becomes prime Barcelona, if prime Barcelona decided to not try to win games, but make their opponents quit playing all together out of a sense of bored frustration. At this point one of two things will happen. The AI will decide it's time to attack, ending either in a goal coming from a shot from a ridiculous angle/location while all your defenders run out of the way, or in an attacker running mindlessly into one of you big strapping centre-backs. Sometimes though, the game decides it's time for you to have a go. At this point, the opponent will pass the ball straight to you. Through no skill of your own, you have possession again.
4. Break the game. You might go back and try step 2 a few times, but it'll always end up the same, so before long you give up. You need to score a goal, as quickly as you possibly can, anything to stop them getting the ball again. Your game plan goes out the window. The hours spend tailoring your possession based, slow build up team becomes pointless. Quick forward passes become the only thing you're interested in. Before you know it, you're a goal up. Exhilarating! All it took, was for you to abandon all the work you put in to the game up to this point. Steps 1-4 repeat themselves now. Something has changed though. Your brain, once focused on battling to win the game, through carefully planned playing style, and well timed tactical and player changes, is concerned with nothing more than keeping the opponent from having the ball at all costs. If they get the ball, you don't get to play. It doesn't really matter how the game goes from here. you might win, you might lose, but either way you feel an overwhelming sense of dissatisfaction. The game simply decided that your choices didn't matter, and funnelled you into playing the way IT wanted you to.

EA Sports FC 26 delivers an overall solid football experience, with smooth gameplay, responsive controls, and an enjoyable attacking flow. The game shines when it comes to building plays, creating chances, and maintaining a fast-paced rhythm that keeps matches engaging.

However, one area where FC 26 struggles is its defensive mechanics.

Defending often feels inconsistent and, at times, frustrating. A major issue is how predictable attacking movements can still break through the defense with ease. Even when you clearly anticipate the opponent’s direction or passing lane, your defenders frequently fail to react effectively. This creates situations where attackers can simply glide past defenders without much resistance.

The problem isn’t just about difficulty—it’s about control. Good defending should reward anticipation and positioning, but in FC 26, those efforts don’t always translate into successful stops. As a result, conceding goals can feel less like a mistake and more like a limitation of the system.

Despite this flaw, the game remains enjoyable, especially for players who prefer attacking football. But for a more balanced and realistic experience, improvements in defensive responsiveness, AI positioning, and tackling reliability are definitely needed.

EA Sports, it's the same.

FIFA or now known as EA FC was one of my favourite sports titles of all time, however thier focus on ultimate team has taken away any significant improvement from the overall game into yearly patches.

Ultimate Team has been the same since 2017 with the exception of evolutions and while they brought back tournaments to online, single player only has squad battles and moments that are played out like tutorials. It is unfortunate you are punished for playing single player and are excluded from certain challenges and content such as tournaments. Online Ultimate Team is still a pay to win system where you invest money to have the best cards to win games - which have zero value at the end of the year.

Career Mode additions are fun, however animations specifc to manager mode has been the same since FIFA 19 and the new icons feature is locked behind other game modes and can be difficult to achieve without purchasing a battle pass, yes a BATTLE PASS in a full priced game. Create a club and player customization is great, but was added a few titles ago and once again is a recycled feature from previous games. It can also be improved with image uploads and face scans which 2K does as fan service and helps with immersion signficiantly. 

The animations look great and it is awesome what HyperMotion can do. On the downside, the players feel slugglish, slow and non-responsive in exchange for complete animations - for instance I can wiggle the left stick left and right slightly and rather than little touches the player will not turn until a certain angle is reached to maintain its animation. The "simulation" slider makes this even worse and is unplayable.

I can never justify pre-ordering this game as it actually incentivizes Ultimate Team players to buy it later in the season due to the more accessible market and bonuses. Maybe I've been playing this game for too long but I've realized years ago that this game is best enjoyed as a casual player as I've exhuasted all my football fantasies in Career Mode. I also refuse to participate in a "compeitive" game that is a pay-to-win rat race where the cards you spent hours grinding become obselete within weeks due to a rapidly changing power curve. 

TL;DR A solid football experience if it is on sale, but too much microtransactions and a lack of changes to engage a player long-term.

I have been coming back to FIFA since 2020, and honestly, I am still not entirely sure why but that itself says something.
Let me be upfront: I do not watch football. Not a single match. Yet here I am, still booting up FC after a long day at work, and somehow knowing the names of players across the biggest clubs in the world. That is the quiet power this game has.
My relationship with the FIFA/FC has not been linear. There were stretches where the quality dipped noticeably and I walked away entirely. But something nostalgia, habit, or maybe just the particular itch this game scratches always pulled me back. I think that is worth acknowledging in any honest review.
What keeps me here is not what you might expect. I do not grind ranked matches or care about climbing leaderboards. What I do is Squad Battle matches and SBCs and I find them genuinely, almost medditatively satisfying. There is something deeply enjoyable about starting with nothing, browsing the store for players, checking their chemistry links, and slowly piecing together a squad that works. The mix-and-match puzzle of building a team with perfect chemistry scratches the same part of my brain that enjoys a good strategy game or even a jigsaw puzzle.
After a long day at work, this is my wind-down routine. Not a thriller, not a shooter just quietly sorting through player cards, experimenting with formations, and finding that one missing piece that completes the squad. It is low-stakes and deeply satisfying in a way that is hard to articulate.
As a bonus, and this genuinely surprised me I have become reasonably informed about real football players purely through osmosis. I know who plays for which club, who the standout performers are, and when a big transfer has happened, simply because the game reflects it. For someone who has never watched a match, that is a neat side effect.
Is it a perfect game? No. EA's monetisation model is aggressive, and the periods where I quit were not accidental the game does go through phases of feeling cynically designed around squeezing your wallet rather than rewarding your time.
But for the specific niche I inhabit the casual Ultimate Team builder who just wants a satisfying loop at the end of the day FC delivers something few other games do. It is part puzzle game, part card collector, part football encyclopedia. And I keep coming back to it, so it must be doing something right.

ما زالت المحركات تعاني من ثغرات قاتلة (Glitches) يستغلها البعض لتحقيق انتصارات غير مستحقة:

    قلتشات الحركة: انزلاقات غير واقعية للاعبين تجعل الدفاع مستحيلاً.

I’m gonna be real — I don’t even touch Football Ultimate Team that much.

What keeps me coming back to EA SPORTS FC™ 26 is Player Career Mode. That mode is just different.

It actually feels like I’m living out my own football journey — starting as a young player, grinding for minutes, improving stats, transferring clubs… it legit feels like I’m writing my own legacy. Every match, every goal, every decision feels personal. It’s super immersive, and I honestly spend most of my time here instead of FUT.

That said… I really wish the game still had the FIFA World Cup partnership. It kinda sucks not having that official tournament vibe anymore. And yeah, the licensing issues are still annoying — not having teams like AC Milan fully licensed just feels off.

Pros:
	•	Player Career Mode is immersive and super rewarding
	•	Feels like you’re building your own football legend
	•	Gameplay is more realistic and slower-paced (in a good way)
	•	Solid atmosphere and match presentation
	•	Great if you prefer offline/single-player experience

Cons:
	•	No FIFA World Cup content anymore (big L honestly)
	•	Licensing issues with some clubs (breaks immersion a bit)
	•	Ultimate Team still feels grindy / kinda pay-to-win
	•	Career mode improvements aren’t huge year-to-year
	•	UI can be clunky at times

Final thoughts:
If you’re like me and just wanna focus on your own career instead of sweating in FUT, this game is 100% worth it. It’s not perfect, but the immersion in Player Career Mode really carries the experience.

Não importa o quão bom você seja ou o quão forte seja o seu time o jogo simplesmente decide quem vai ganhar. É nítido. Tem partidas em que nada funciona pra você: passes errados sem motivo, jogadores lentos do nada, finalizações bizarras, o van dijk ou qualquer outro zagueiro foda perdendo na disputa de corpo contra uma Cláudia pina ou qualquer outra mulher, enquanto o adversário, mesmo com um time pior, parece ter tudo favorecendo.

Please, absolutely go out of your way to buy this flawlessly designed, calming, and incredibly consumer-friendly experience. It’s a shining example of what happens when a company clearly tests every detail of their game with care, precision, and deep love for the people playing it.

I’m mainly a Career Mode player, and I just have to applaud a few of the *outstanding* features we’ve been gifted:

Live start point with Marseille: you’re dropped 10 points behind PSG with 8 games left, and the board expects you to win the league. Naturally, even if you win every single match, PSG, being the charitable and inconsistent side they are, refuse to drop points. You get sacked for not achieving what is essentially a statistical miracle. Truly groundbreaking realism. 

The match notification popup is a stroke of genius, blocking the top-left of the pitch for a generous 5 seconds. It really enhances immersion by making sure you can’t see what’s happening during key moments. Vision is overrated anyway.

You can’t train composure on created players, which is fantastic because it reinforces the idea that players are born mentally fragile and must remain that way forever. 

Authentic simulation mode (Legendary) is an absolute joy. Passing feels beautifully unpredictable, simple 5-yard passes become thrilling gambles, and through balls, even when gently tapped,travel at the speed of light. Crosses and lobbed balls are so refined they’ve been elevated to an abstract art form.

The opposition AI is a tactical marvel. If you defend well, they’ll reward you by passing around the back for the entire 90 minutes. It’s less of a football match and more of a meditative exercise.

And of course, the way difficulty increases is pure genius. Instead of making the AI smarter, your own players simply lose all basic cognitive function. Suddenly, controlling the ball becomes optional, passing becomes theoretical, and any form of composure disappears the moment a defender exists in your general vicinity. 

Thank you so much for this unforgettable experience. I would say it’s once in a lifetime, but thankfully you deliver this same level of excellence every single year. 

Your truly,

I have 4 hours in this game.

Technically.

Emotionally? Spiritually? Across timelines and platforms like some sort of football multiverse traveler? It’s closer to 200 hours if you add Xbox Series, PS5, and whatever dimension Manager Mode exists in. Time is not linear when you’re negotiating contracts at 1:13AM.

Let’s start with Manager Career Mode.

I load in thinking I am a tactical mastermind. I adjust formations like I know what “false nine” means. I absolutely do not. I just move the little circles around until the vibes feel correct. Suddenly I’m yelling at my monitor because my left-back didn’t overlap properly, even though I personally told him to do something vague like “balanced attack.” What does that mean? Nobody knows. Not even him.

But I get LOST in it. Transfers. Youth academy. Press conferences where I say things that feel correct but probably destroy morale. I promise a player more game time and immediately forget he exists. I am running a football club like it’s a chaotic family business and I am the cousin who somehow got promoted.

And yet… it works.

There’s something about building a squad from “mid-table sadness” to “champions league delusion” that just consumes me. I’ll simulate one match. Then I’ll manually play the next. Then suddenly I’m deeply invested in whether my 17-year-old regen striker becomes a legend or a disappointment.

Now. The other modes.

They are… there.

I enter them. I look around. I leave. It’s not that they’re bad. It’s that my brain simply decides, “No thank you.” It’s like going to a buffet and only eating the same dish every time. Am I limiting myself? Yes. Will I change? Absolutely not.

But Pro Clubs.

Oh.

Pro Clubs is different. Pro Clubs is memories. It’s laughter. It’s your friend insisting he’s a RW but playing like a lost right-back. It’s someone calling for the ball nonstop. It’s chaotic teamwork and questionable decision-making. And I miss that dearly. There is something magical about all of you controlling one chaotic little digital footballer each, running around like synchronized confusion.

Even with only 4 hours on Steam, this game feels familiar. Like putting on boots you’ve worn for years. I may not fully understand half the tactical sliders. I may confidently explain mechanics that I absolutely do not grasp. But I am there. I am managing. I am adjusting formations based purely on intuition and caffeine.

9/10.

I don’t know what I’m doing.
But I’m doing it confidently.

EA Sports FC 26 is a genuinely good football game if we judge it purely based on its gameplay and do not compare it with any previous titles. The game makes a noticeable step forward in terms of realism and visual sharpness when recreating the atmosphere of a football stadium. The lighting, pitch details, and overall presentation feel more authentic, making matches look closer to real-life broadcasts.

One of the most impressive improvements in FC 26 is the animation system. Player movements feel smoother and more natural than ever before. New animations for dribbling, passing, and physical interactions between players add a sense of fluidity that makes the gameplay more immersive. Compared to earlier football games in general, the transitions between actions are much cleaner, which helps the match flow feel more realistic and dynamic.

However, despite these positive aspects, FC 26 suffers from extremely poor optimization. Even when comparing it to EA Sports FC 25, which was released only one year earlier, FC 26 feels significantly less stable in terms of performance. Many players experience random stuttering, frame drops, and sudden lag during gameplay.

What makes the issue more frustrating is that the game may run perfectly fine at the beginning of a session. The performance is stable and smooth at first, but after playing for a while, unexplained stutters and slowdowns begin to appear. This happens even on systems that exceed the official system requirements of the game. As a result, the experience can become inconsistent and sometimes frustrating, especially during longer play sessions.

Because of this, the game clearly needs better optimization to meet the expectations of players. Improving performance stability would significantly enhance the overall experience and help the game attract and retain more players in the long term.

Overall, I would rate FC 26 6.5 out of 10. The core gameplay is enjoyable and the improvements in realism and animation are very promising. However, the score could be much higher if the developers focus on listening to player feedback and delivering better performance optimization in future updates.

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐ (2.5 / 5)

"Same pitch, different year—but still keeps me coming back."

The Good
As someone who started this journey with FC 24, I still find a lot to love about the core gameplay. If you enjoy football, the hook is definitely still there.

Rush Mode (The Highlight): This is a standout for me. It’s a completely new experience that wasn't in FC 24, and I’ve really enjoyed it. It adds a fresh dynamic to the game that breaks up the usual grind.

Addictive Gameplay Loops: The daily and weekly rewards are a huge draw. Whether it’s Squad Battles or the Ultimate Team tournaments, there is always a reason to log in. The seasonal objectives and rewards keep me occupied and motivated to build a better squad.

New Additions: The new modes and updated season structures add a bit of fresh air to the experience.

Fun Factor: At its heart, it’s still fun to collect players and hit the pitch.

The Bad
While I enjoy the game, it’s hard to ignore that it feels like a copy-paste of FC 24 and FC 25.

Lack of Innovation: It feels very much like "the usual same thing." For a full-priced release, I expected more of a jump in quality or feel.

Defense & Scripting: The defense is incredibly hard to break down to the point where it feels pre-planned. Sometimes it feels like the game has already decided who is going to win before the whistle blows. The AI defensive positioning can feel like hitting a brick wall.

Final Verdict
It’s a solid game if you love football and the grind of Ultimate Team, the addition of Rush Mode is a great step forward and a lot of fun, but the lack of significant changes and the frustrating defensive mechanics hold it back. It’s a 2.5/5 for me—good for a fun time, but definitely needs work on the balancing.

You see the run before the defenders do.
You place the pass before they react.
And by the time the goalkeeper understands what happened, the crowd is already celebrating.

Confident. Clean.

EA SPORTS FC 26 is a modern football simulation developed by EA Canada and EA Romania and published by Electronic Arts on Steam. As part of Electronic Arts’ long-running football series that evolved from the former FIFA franchise, the game continues to refine its formula of realistic match simulation, strategic depth, and expansive career and online modes. With each yearly release the series aims to improve gameplay authenticity while maintaining accessibility for both casual players and competitive football fans, and EA SPORTS FC 26 continues that tradition with a blend of mechanical improvements, presentation upgrades, and expanded tactical control.

The foundation of the experience lies in the core gameplay mechanics that simulate real football matches. Player movement feels smoother and more natural than in previous installments, with improved ball physics and animation transitions allowing dribbling, passing, and shooting to flow together more seamlessly. The dribbling system rewards precision and timing, giving skilled players the ability to perform quick changes of direction, close control touches, and skill moves that replicate the agility of real-world footballers. Passing has also been refined, encouraging players to think carefully about spacing and positioning when constructing attacking plays.

Shooting mechanics place greater emphasis on shot selection and positioning rather than relying solely on power and timing. Players must consider angles, defensive pressure, and the movement of the goalkeeper before attempting to score. These adjustments add a layer of tactical realism that makes goals feel more rewarding when they are the result of well-constructed attacking sequences. Meanwhile, defensive gameplay focuses more heavily on anticipation and positioning, requiring players to read the opponent’s intentions and intercept passes or challenge attackers at the right moment.

Tactical systems in EA SPORTS FC 26 provide deeper control over how teams behave during matches. Players can customize formations, adjust pressing intensity, and modify attacking strategies to suit different styles of play. This level of control allows managers to experiment with approaches ranging from high-pressure counterattacks to slower possession-based strategies. The tactical interface makes it possible to adapt quickly to the flow of a match, giving players the ability to change formations or adjust defensive lines without interrupting gameplay.

Artificial intelligence improvements also contribute to the authenticity of matches. Teammates make more intelligent runs off the ball and react more effectively to changes in possession. Defenders track attackers with greater awareness, making it more difficult to exploit predictable patterns in the defense. These adjustments help create matches that feel more organic and less scripted, as both teams dynamically respond to evolving situations on the field.

Presentation remains one of the most impressive aspects of the series. Stadiums are recreated with remarkable attention to detail, featuring animated crowds, realistic lighting, and broadcast-style camera work that mirrors real football coverage. Player models are built using high-quality facial scans and advanced motion capture animations, capturing the distinctive movements and celebrations of real-life athletes. The combination of visual fidelity and broadcast presentation makes every match feel like a televised sporting event.

Beyond standard matches, the game offers a wide range of modes designed to keep players engaged for long periods. Career Mode continues to be a major feature, allowing players to control either a club manager or an individual footballer. Manager Career focuses on building a successful team through transfers, youth development, and tactical planning, while Player Career follows the journey of a single athlete rising through the ranks of professional football. Both paths offer multiple seasons of progression and evolving storylines.

Another prominent mode is Ultimate Team, where players assemble squads by collecting player cards representing athletes from leagues around the world. By participating in matches and completing challenges, players earn rewards that allow them to strengthen their teams. This mode emphasizes customization and long-term progression, offering a constantly evolving roster-building experience that has become one of the series’ most popular features.

Online multiplayer also plays a central role in the game’s longevity. Competitive modes allow players to face opponents from across the globe in ranked matches, tournaments, and seasonal competitions. The online environment adds an unpredictable element to matches as players encounter a wide variety of playstyles and strategies.

The audio design further enhances immersion. Commentary teams provide real-time analysis and reactions to events on the field, while stadium crowds respond dynamically to goals, fouls, and dramatic saves. This aspect remains one of the most debated elements of the series.

Despite these concerns, EA SPORTS FC 26 remains one of the most comprehensive football simulations available. Its combination of refined gameplay mechanics, realistic presentation, and numerous modes ensures that players have multiple ways to experience the sport. Whether guiding a club through a long managerial career, building a dream team of international stars, or competing online against skilled opponents, the game offers a rich and varied football experience.

Overall, EA SPORTS FC 26 continues the evolution of Electronic Arts’ football simulation franchise with improved mechanics, deeper tactical systems, and polished presentation. While the monetization model may not appeal to every player, the core gameplay remains engaging and authentic, capturing the excitement and strategic depth of the sport.

FC 26 é a continuação da fase “pós-FIFA” da EA, agora consolidada como EA SPORTS FC.
A proposta é manter o trono dos simuladores de futebol com mais realismo e controle.
A jogabilidade está mais fluida e responsiva que nas versões anteriores.
Os movimentos parecem menos “robotizados” e mais naturais.
Há dois estilos de gameplay: competitivo e autêntico.
O modo competitivo é mais rápido e direto.
O modo autêntico valoriza ritmo real e construção tática.
Os PlayStyles deixam jogadores realmente diferentes entre si.
Craques se destacam de forma perceptível em campo.
O modo Carreira recebeu melhorias em profundidade e imersão.
Ultimate Team continua sendo o modo mais popular.
Mas também é o mais criticado pela comunidade.
Menus ainda podem apresentar lentidão.
Servidores online sofrem instabilidade em horários de pico.
Alguns jogadores reclamam da inconsistência dos goleiros.
A IA defensiva às vezes parece irregular.
Visualmente o jogo continua muito bonito.
Licenças oficiais seguem sendo um dos grandes atrativos.
É um pacote robusto para quem ama futebol virtual.
No geral, evolui bem, mas ainda depende de atualizações para atingir seu máximo potencial.

I do not regret to express my significant disappointment with the current state of EA Sports FC 26. Based on my experience, the overall quality and performance of the game do not justify its purchase, even when offered at a 50% discount.

The most critical concern remains server stability. Persistent connectivity issues, inconsistent matchmaking performance, and unreliable online responsiveness continue to undermine the gameplay experience, particularly within Ultimate Team (FUT). For a title that places substantial emphasis on online competitive modes and live service engagement, the lack of consistent server performance is unacceptable.

Furthermore, the overall game state reflects minimal meaningful improvement compared to previous releases. The recurring technical shortcomings, combined with gameplay frustrations and monetization fatigue, contribute to a sense of stagnation rather than progression. Unfortunately, this has been a recurring issue year after year.

For players considering purchasing the game, I would strongly advise reconsidering or not at all, especially if the primary interest lies in Ultimate Team or other competitive online modes. If you chooses to purchase, it may be more worthwhile to wait until the end part of the season and focus on Pro Clubs with friends, which tends to provide a comparatively more enjoyable and less commercially pressured experience. However, even in this mode, server instability remains a concern same with last year.

In its current condition or may be ever, FC26 does not meet the expected standards of quality, reliability, or value for money. As a long-time player of the franchise, this level of recurring underperformance is disappointing.

Overall Rating: 0/10

I honestly regret buying FC 26. The marketing made it sound like this was going to be the biggest upgrade in years  smarter AI, realistic physics, better career mode depth, revamped Ultimate Team features, improved servers the whole package. And for about a week, it actually felt promising.

Then everything changed.

Features they hyped up in trailers and deep dives were either quietly toned down or straight-up removed after the first week. The “dynamic AI behavior” suddenly feels identical to last year. The new gameplay sliders and customization options? Gone or locked behind updates that made no sense. Career mode improvements feel half-baked and buggy. Ultimate Team content got reduced, rewards adjusted, and suddenly the grind got worse.

Servers were unstable at launch, which is almost expected at this point, but instead of improving, matchmaking somehow feels worse. Input delay is back, defensive AI feels inconsistent, and the so-called “realistic physics” seems to have vanished after the first patch.

It feels like we bought one version of the game during early access and then got a downgraded version after launch week. Communication has been minimal, patch notes are vague, and there’s zero transparency about why features changed.

At this point, FC 26 feels more like a live-service experiment than a finished football game. Broken promises, reduced features, and the same old issues underneath a new title.

If this is the direction the series is heading, longtime fans have every reason to be frustrated.

I don’t even know where to start with FC 26, because calling this a “finished game” feels like calling instant noodles a five-star gourmet meal. Sure, it exists, technically, but you know deep down something went very wrong.

First of all, the gameplay feels like my players just finished eating three large pizzas and decided football was optional. Turning takes about three to five business days. By the time my defender reacts, the opponent has already scored, celebrated, gone home, started a family, and retired.

The passing system is a social experiment. I aim left, the ball goes right. I tap gently, my player launches it into orbit. I hold power, and he passes it like he’s apologizing to the grass. I’m not controlling footballers — I’m negotiating with chaos.

And don’t even get me started on the AI. My defenders politely escort attackers to the goal like they’re VIP guests. “Right this way, sir, would you like us to move out of the way completely?” Meanwhile, my striker couldn’t finish his dinner, let alone a 1-on-1.

The physics are incredible, if the goal was to simulate players wearing wet jeans and ice skates. Tackles bounce randomly, rebounds always go to the opponent, and my goalkeeper has the reaction speed of a sleeping sloth.

The menus? Oh, beautiful. Not visually — I mean they give you plenty of time to reflect on your life while waiting for them to load. I’ve aged mentally every time I try to open Ultimate Team.

And scripting? I refuse to believe it doesn’t exist. My team goes from prime Barcelona in the first half to a group of strangers who just met in a parking lot in the second.

Overall, FC 26 isn’t a football game. It’s a stress simulator. It’s a test of patience. It’s a reminder that disappointment can, in fact, be purchased digitally.

First of all, congratulations. It genuinely takes a special level of talent to charge $70 for a “premium” game and then deliver an online experience that functions like it’s being powered by a hamster on life support. Truly impressive stuff.

I especially appreciate paying full price just to stare at disconnect messages, lag spikes, and broken servers. Nothing says “next-gen gaming” quite like wondering whether I’ll actually finish a match before your infrastructure collapses again. What the hell am I paying for? Because it sure as ♥♥♥♥ isn’t stability, reliability, or competence.

And let’s talk about the business model — pure genius. Advertise online play as a core feature, sell millions of copies, make the experience borderline unusable for a chunk of your player base, and then lock refunds behind policies that ensure we’re stuck with this broken mess. If this isn’t a scam, it’s doing a phenomenal impression of one. I’m trapped with a $70 product that doesn’t work as advertised. Outstanding work.

Even more impressive is the yearly “innovation.” Every year, I foolishly expect meaningful upgrades. Instead, features disappear. Modes get stripped. Content gets watered down. And then the same recycled ♥♥♥♥ is repackaged as if it’s revolutionary. It’s almost artistic — removing things people love and then pretending you did us a favor. Bold strategy.

And of course, the microtransactions. Because clearly $70 wasn’t enough. Why stop there? Let’s squeeze players for every extra dollar possible while the base game struggles to function properly. It’s honestly breathtaking how shameless it feels.

What really makes this sting is that I’ve been buying your games like a complete idiot for six straight years. Six years of giving you the benefit of the doubt. Six years of thinking, “Surely they’ll fix their ♥♥♥♥ this time.” Six years of loyalty rewarded with the same broken servers, the same removed features, the same recycled nonsense. That’s on me — lesson learned.

At this point, it’s hard not to feel embarrassed for a company of your size and resources delivering something this sloppy while charging a premium price. You’re not an indie studio scraping by — you’re a massive corporation. And yet this is the standard? You should be ashamed that this is what passes for a finished product.

I’m done handing over my money for this half-baked, overpriced, cash-grab circus. Fix your damn servers. Stop gutting features. Stop charging full price for unfinished ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. And maybe — just maybe — start acting like a company that takes pride in what it puts out.

As background, my experience with FIFA and the like is that I jumped from FIFA 2006 to EA FC 24 and then to EA FC 26. FC 26 suffers from a lot of the same problems as EA FC 24, namely several glaring glitches that make the game incredibly frustrating to play. For instance, the game will randomly experience a catastrophic drop in frame rate making a match practically unplayable. This is especially infuriating in a squad battle or rivals game where you really need the game to perform reliably. I've experienced instances where my custom control settings get corrupted where certain actions simply don't work, like clicking R3 to flick the ball up. Other weird glitches that have not been fixed since FC 24 include  "recommended" graphic settings producing low frame rates, drop down menus of players that have been changed out not disappearing when you start entering the late phases of a match, odd hair color glitches where player and fan models have neon hair colors, and ultimate team games just disconnecting and you being given a loss for the disconnection. A problem unique to FC 26 is the likely AI generated crowd models repeating themselves where you see twins or triplets of different people in the crowds.

         I have yet to take a look at the player career mode for this game (once I do might revisit this review), but I recall FC 24 suffering from the problem of an incredibly boring investment system that had you wasting money on such things as "buy a yacht" and having a lackluster personality system that locked you out of different abilities because you couldn't go back an reallocate points to unlock them. I honestly don't have much faith that things have changed, but again I will return to this review if they have.

         I've played a lot of FC 24 and 26 because I enjoy football. But spending any of your gameplay time mindlessly opening card packs that give you a less than 1% chance to get good quality players, dealing with unacceptable glitches, and a steep learning curve that isn't intuitive to new members of the community make it extremely difficult to recommend this game in good faith. A game series that has been in existence for this long does not have any excuse for being so hostile to the player in its design plagued by negligence and lack of care. The tag line "EA finally listened" should not be a point of pride attached to this game. Instead, fans should take it as damning evidence that this company believes that the bare minimum of listening to the fan base's criticism and feedback is too high a bar for them on a normal day when it is in fact the lowest hanging fruit in the gaming industry.

          FC represents a lot of the worst of what gaming has to offer. I can only hope that they one day gain the wisdom that a game should not be a yearly release if it means putting out a low quality product. But history has shown that having faith in EA is guaranteed to be met with disappointment.

This gaming franchise has gone from by far the best football/soccer video gaming experience to absolute garbage. It's really sad to say having played FIFA since 09 and FUT since 11. The Devs really got my hopes up at the beginning of the game cycle because they were "listening to community feedback." However, as soon as the pro players and everyone who is willing to buy FIFA points complained, they reverted back and completely forgot what they were going differently than the past couple of years.

The game play has gotten so unrealistic and the game holds your hand so much with the AI defending. All of the broken mechanics in this game make it so hard to play and enjoy anymore. I know making a video game realistic especially when it comes to an actual sport because there is so many unpredictable variables, but its like they didn't even try. They just slap on the same name and change the number every year but change nothing with the actual gameplay or mechanics. And don't even get me started on the stupid playstyles. They have completely ruined cards. I remember when getting a card that had all 80s stats meant something, now just need a bronze card with Finesse+ and you can score from anywhere. Playstyles have been the worst addition in recent years. And the power curve still didn't change, like they said it would.

Some ideas that they NEED to do in order to make this game enjoyable again would be:

1. REMOVE playstyles and roles completely (My 90+ CM that has 90+ Passing should be able to make a 10 yard pass, just because they don't have Tiki Taka doesn't mean that their passing stats are irrelevant)
2. Actually make the power curve slower (We don't need a promo every single week, promos are actually killing the game, there are way too many cards in this game anymore. There should only be a handful of promos every game cycle. TOTY, TOTS, TOTT, FS, RTTK, and FUTTIES. TOTW, MOTM, and POTM cards are also completely fine. EVOs, are enough already on top of the millions of other cards that we get, we sill see the same 20 players on everyone's teams already. The only reason as to why we have so many promos is so that they can keep cleaning out everyone's wallets, it's actually so pathetic)
3. Make the gameplay feel responsive and fun again (I'm no coder or software engineer, however, for all the money that this company has, it's mind-blowing as to how this game can never have something that absolutely breaks the game and doesn't ruin it. Every update they "fix" something, but then make the gameplay worse and add two more broken mechanics and then we don't get a patch for 2 months. There are SO many other studios and developers that have WAY LESS people and WAY LESS money and make a better game all round)
4. Bring back the old reward system from champs (make rewards come out on Thursdays again instead of instant gratification, this actually gave you something to look forward to instead of people going out and finishing their champs games and flooding the market, the market is already ruined. Plus when the rewards were on Thursdays, you probably thought you had a terrible weekend league, couple days do bye and now you get your rewards, look you get something good out of them)
5. Balance the Men and Women competing against each other (I'm all for having the women in the game. It adds to much more to the game. However, when comparing stats between the men and women, some stats make absolutely no sense at all. I think that they should have 3 versions for all game modes to compensate for this. I mean, they should have an all men's, all women's, and a combined men's and women's game modes for each of champs, rivals, and squad battles. And yes, I understand that when women were introduced into FIFA several years ago, it was only in kick off, and not many people played that. But, Pina should never be bodying VVD and Rio, that just would never happen IRL)
6. Stop trying to make this an E-Sports game (the gameplay is way too unpredictable to be considered an E-Sports game. You have to have certain that when you take a shot on goal from 10 yards out that it's going to go into the same sport 100 times out of 100. If not then stop and figure out which route you want to take with this game. Either E-Sports or for the casual football/soccer fans)

If they really want to bring bad the joy of this game instead of catering towards E-Sports and the rich, they really need to take a step back and make some changes going forward. Like I said I have been playing this game for over 10 years, but certain decisions have seriously hurt this game. Because I know how good this game could be and it's so frustrating to see and play anymore. So, if you are thinking of getting this game, as of right now, DON'T! Save your money and find something else that can make you feel the same fun and enjoyment. Since video games are supposed to be played for fun and relaxation!

I went into EA Sports FC 26 hoping it would pull me back in, especially since I hadn’t played this style of football game in several years. Unfortunately, I got bored far quicker than expected.

For context, I have been playing Football Manager, so it’s not like I’m disconnected from football games entirely. That might actually be part of the problem. After spending time with a game that offers depth, strategy, and long-term engagement, EA Sports FC 26 felt shallow by comparison. Even allowing for the fact that they’re very different types of games, FC 26 just didn’t give me much reason to stay invested.

The core gameplay loop started to feel repetitive almost immediately. Matches blended together, and despite waiting for something to hook me — a new mechanic, a sense of progression, or even just that “one more match” feeling — it never really arrived. What surprised me most is that even after years away from the series, it still felt overly familiar, and not in a comforting way.

The presentation is polished and technically fine, but polish alone doesn’t carry the experience. Once the initial novelty wears off, there’s very little that feels fresh or engaging unless you’re already committed to grinding the usual modes. As someone coming back with relatively fresh eyes, I expected more.

Overall, EA Sports FC 26 failed to hold my attention, and I stopped playing much sooner than I anticipated. Even with time away from the series — and an ongoing interest in football through Football Manager — this just didn’t feel engaging or rewarding. If you’re hoping it will reignite your interest in football games, it may end up feeling stale surprisingly fast.

The Paradox: Sophisticated on Paper, Boring in Practice

I've played FC 24 and FC 25 for over 400hrs combined. So when this one launched, I was genuinely excited. The gameplay [i]felt[/i] more visceral. The hype was real.

But after 150hrs? It's the [i]least fun[/i] of the three.

[list]
[*] Goalkeepers were buffed — but at the cost of everything else
[*] Longshots were essentially killed off
[*] Goal variety has decreased, not increased
[*] Multiplayer (both UT & Clubs) gets boring [i]fast[/i]
[*] Career Mode on Ultimate difficulty is surprisingly easy to beat
[/list]

---------------------------------------

CAREER MODE: MISSED POTENTIAL

The new career features [i]seemed[/i] cool on paper. But instead of giving you a "this is your story" vibe, it feels like:

[b]Do your chores.[/b] Earn a jersey you won't care about.

A great concept, sloppily executed — it's clear the implementation wasn't built with [i]fun[/i] as the priority.

---------------------------------------

THE MOD PARADOX

After trying Anth James gameplay mods, I can confirm: the experience is [i]there[/i] — but buried under unpolished systems and unclear direction from the developers.

I managed to get the game exactly to where I want it to be...

...by using [b]mods[/b].

---------------------------------------

TL;DR: Good bones, sloppy execution, requires mods to be good, and even modded the AI's too easy. Pass until community patches breathe life into it.

Pasele simple de 2 metri devin aventuri epice, iar portarii fie apără imposibilul, fie se uită la minge ca la un documentar pe Discovery.

Serverele sunt probabil alimentate de un router din 2009 ascuns într-un beci. Lagul apare exact când ești singur cu portarul – moment în care jocul decide că este momentul perfect să îți transforme atacantul într-un dansator de balet confuz.

Matchmaking-ul? Absolut genial. După două meciuri relaxate, sistemul te aruncă direct cu cineva care joacă de parcă are contract cu NASA pentru testarea reflexelor umane. Evident, echipa lui valorează cât o mașină second-hand în FIFA Points.

Și să nu uităm de „surprizele” din Ultimate Team: deschizi pachete, vezi animații dramatice, lumini, focuri de artificii… și apare un fundaș de 83 pe care l-ai primit deja de 14 ori. Mulțumim, Electronic Arts, pentru această experiență emoțională profundă.

AI-ul coechipierilor este și el impresionant: fundașii se feresc elegant din calea adversarului, iar mijlocașii privesc faza de parcă au bilete VIP în primul rând.

Pe scurt, EA FC 26 este acel joc care te face să spui „mai joc un meci” chiar dacă ultimele cinci te-au făcut să îți pui serios întrebări despre sensul vieții. Frustrant, dezechilibrat și uneori complet absurd – dar suficient de captivant încât să revii… doar ca să fii din nou nervos peste 10 minute. 🎮⚽
